projects.title: Into The Unknown, Book Design
projects.summary: Cover, interior layout and identity for an illustrated book.
projects.description: A self-initiated book project titled Into The Unknown, covering cover design, interior layout, and a series of full-bleed illustrated spreads. The identity leans on bold type and quiet negative space to let the imagery carry the narrative.

outcome.title: Final Cover
outcome.text: The final cover pairs a centered display wordmark with a moody, large-format illustration. The choice of a single dominant image anchors the identity so the interior spreads can vary in pace without breaking the book's visual voice. The system was carried through to the interior breakdown, with consistent hierarchy, generous margins and restrained type sizing.

timeline.title: First Draft
timeline.text: Opening exploration. The first draft experimented with a landscape-led composition and a lighter typographic treatment. Useful for establishing scale but the title was reading as secondary to the illustration.

timeline.title: Second Iteration
timeline.text: Shift to a heavier, stacked wordmark that could hold its own against the imagery. Introduced a darker color envelope so the cover would pull attention on a crowded shelf.

timeline.title: Third Iteration
timeline.text: Refined spacing, cleaned up the join between the title lockup and the illustration's negative space, and settled on the proportions that carried through to the final cover.

timeline.title: Interior Breakdown
timeline.text: Full interior breakdown showing how the cover's visual language was extended to running heads, chapter openers and image plates inside the book.

projects.title: On Disappearing Games, Argument Machine
projects.summary: A generative argument machine about game preservation, built from Tracery grammars and an ambient p5.js particle poem.
projects.description: Two linked pieces exploring the crisis of game preservation through procedural language. The first is an ambient particle poem in p5.js: action verbs — fall, drop, fly, break, rise — drift down a deep purple canvas, evoking the slow disappearance of interactive works. The second is a Tracery-powered argument generator drawing on 17 game theorists and digital humanities scholars (Huizinga, Bogost, Derrida, Manovich, Stiegler and others): select a thinker to generate a unique argument about bit rot, format obsolescence, server shutdowns, and cultural loss — or trigger a free-form passage from the full grammar. The grammar is grounded in documented events (GameSpy, City of Heroes, P.T., The Crew) and real statistics on the inaccessibility of classic games.
